design_detail: Systematic review and frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42014008976; protocol published) of double-blind randomized trials lasting at least 1 week of oral ADHD medicines given alone (amphetamines including lisdexamfetamine, atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, guanfacine, methylphenidate including dexmethylphenidate, modafinil) against each other or placebo, analysed separately for children and adolescents (5 to 17 years) and for adults. Primary outcomes at the time closest to 12 weeks: clinician-rated change in core ADHD symptoms (in children and adolescents also teacher-rated) and dropouts because of side effects. 133 trials (81 in children and adolescents, 51 in adults, 1 in both). The PDF read is the online-first version (PDF pp. 1–12).
can_establish: Average short-term (about 12 weeks) differences in clinician-rated core ADHD symptoms and in stopping a trial because of side effects for each class of medicine against placebo and, mostly through indirect comparison, between classes, in double-blind trials up to April 2017.
cannot_establish: Long-term benefit or harm (too few trials beyond 12 weeks); the absolute numbers of people who benefit or stop (the article gives only odds ratios and standardized differences); rare harms such as psychosis (not studied); differences between products within a class or by dose; a trial-based head-to-head comparison of amphetamines with methylphenidate in adults (none in the network); effects in people whose other conditions need other medicines (excluded).

sample.recruitment: Searches of PubMed, BIOSIS Previews, CINAHL, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Embase, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, OpenGrey, Web of Science Core Collection, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses (UK and Ireland; abstracts and international) and the WHO International Trials Registry Platform including ClinicalTrials.gov, from inception to 7 April 2017, without language restriction; FDA, EMA and manufacturers' websites and the references of reviews and guidelines hand-searched; study authors and manufacturers contacted for unpublished data (PDF p. 3). 9948 records screened and 3525 full texts assessed (Figure 1, PDF p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Double-blind randomized trials (parallel, crossover or cluster) of at least 1 week in children (5 to 11 years), adolescents (12 to 17) or adults with a primary DSM or ICD diagnosis of ADHD; no restriction by subtype, sex, IQ, socioeconomic status or comorbidity except comorbidities needing other medicines; oral monotherapy compared with another drug or placebo. Enrichment designs (only responders kept after a run-in) were excluded because they may inflate efficacy and tolerability (PDF p. 3). The primary analysis was limited to doses within the therapeutic range, per FDA recommendations where applicable (PDF p. 4), and trials using doses above guideline recommendations were excluded (PDF p. 9).
sample.demographics: Not given in the article; the characteristics of the included trials are in the appendix (pp. 283–381), which was not read.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; leaving a trial because of side effects (tolerability) or for any reason (acceptability) are outcomes.
sample.selection_effects: Only double-blind trials, mostly placebo-controlled and short. Enrichment designs, doses above guidelines, combination therapy and, according to the note to Figure 1, trials including patients with comorbid disorders were excluded (PDF pp. 3, 9). Industry sponsorship of the trials could not be analysed (PDF p. 8). The search ended in April 2017; three eligible trials found in May 2018 were not added (PDF p. 9). Unpublished data were used for 83% of trials (PDF p. 4).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Oral; within FDA-licensed or guideline ranges in the primary analysis. Two dose sensitivity analyses (trials at FDA-licensed doses only; guideline ranges differing from FDA recommendations) confirmed the primary analysis (PDF pp. 4, 8). Doses by product are not shown in the article; lisdexamfetamine was separated from the other amphetamines in a post hoc analysis.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable; trials of single medicines only, combination therapy excluded.

comparison.controls: Placebo or another active medicine within trials; network estimates combine direct and indirect evidence. In children and adolescents some trials compared amphetamines with methylphenidate directly; in adults the network has no direct amphetamine–methylphenidate link, both being connected only to placebo (Figure 2, PDF p. 4).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable within trials. The network assumes transitivity, which the authors defend by saying that participants' previous exposure and response to ADHD medicines were evenly distributed across trials and nodes (PDF p. 9).

outcomes.instruments: Validated rating scales measuring only core ADHD symptoms (list in appendix pp. 273–274, not read), rated by clinicians, teachers, parents or adults themselves; Clinical Global Impression–Improvement (CGI-I); proportion leaving because of any side effect (tolerability) and for any reason (acceptability); change in weight and blood pressure (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: Only validated scales measuring core symptoms were included (PDF pp. 9–10). Risk of bias of trials assessed with the Cochrane tool; certainty with GRADE for network meta-analyses (PDF p. 3).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy: standardized mean difference (Hedges' g) in symptom change; tolerability and acceptability: odds ratios. In Table 1 negative values favour the drug in the row; in Table 2 odds ratios above 1 favour the drug in the column (PDF pp. 6–7).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (3 primary and 6 secondary outcomes, two age groups, every pairwise comparison).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; the included trials were double-blind. Data were extracted by at least two independent investigators (PDF p. 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Network estimates at about 12 weeks (certainty by GRADE). Clinician-rated symptoms against placebo: amphetamines SMD −1.02 (95% CI −1.19 to −0.85) in children and adolescents and −0.79 (−0.99 to −0.58) in adults; methylphenidate −0.78 (−0.93 to −0.62) and −0.49 (−0.64 to −0.35); all four moderate. Amphetamines against methylphenidate: −0.24 (−0.44 to −0.05) in children and adolescents and −0.29 (−0.54 to −0.05) in adults, both low. Teacher ratings in children and adolescents: methylphenidate −0.82 (−1.16 to −0.48, low) against placebo; no data for amphetamines. Dropouts because of side effects against placebo: amphetamines OR 2.30 (1.36 to 3.89) in children and adolescents and 3.26 (1.54 to 6.92) in adults (moderate); methylphenidate 1.44 (0.90 to 2.31, low) and 2.39 (1.40 to 4.08, high). Amphetamines against methylphenidate: OR 1.60 (0.94 to 2.73, low) in children and adolescents and 1.36 (0.54 to 3.43, very low) in adults. Acceptability against placebo: methylphenidate in children and adolescents OR 0.69 (0.52 to 0.91); amphetamines in adults 0.68 (0.49 to 0.95). Weight against placebo (SMD): amphetamines −0.71 (−1.15 to −0.27) and −0.60 (−1.03 to −0.18); methylphenidate −0.77 (−1.09 to −0.45) and −0.74 (−1.20 to −0.28). Systolic blood pressure: amphetamines in children and adolescents SMD 0.09 (0.01 to 0.18); methylphenidate in adults 0.17 (0.05 to 0.30). Diastolic: amphetamines 0.21 (0.12 to 0.31) and methylphenidate 0.24 (0.14 to 0.33) in the younger group (see reporting issues on the age group printed), methylphenidate 0.20 (0.08 to 0.32) in adults. Common heterogeneity SD in children and adolescents 0.355 (teacher ratings), 0.188 (clinician ratings) and 0.268 (tolerability); in adults 0.178 and 0.282; no significant global inconsistency. No absolute event rates are given in the article.
analysis.covariates: None at review level. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses for study length, comorbidities, IQ, crossover design, unfair dose comparisons and data imputation were reported as generally robust (appendix pp. 479–491, not read); gender, age (children against adolescents), low risk of bias, medication status and industry sponsorship could not be assessed for lack of data (PDF p. 8).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42014008976; protocol published (BMJ Open 2017, reference 30); PRISMA extension for network meta-analyses followed (PDF p. 3). Changes to the original protocol are listed in the appendix (p. 25, not read); the lisdexamfetamine analysis was post hoc; planned analyses at 26 and 52 weeks and several planned subgroups could not be done (PDF pp. 4, 8, 10).
analysis.selective_reporting: Many results are only in the appendix: the pairwise meta-analyses and their heterogeneity, the amphetamine-versus-methylphenidate CGI-I estimate (described in the Discussion as no significant difference, without numbers), parent and self ratings by drug pair, blood-pressure estimates between drugs, the dose analyses and the funnel plots.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The authors note that some nodes of the network included few trials and that actual head-to-head trials were few (PDF p. 9).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In trials of about 12 weeks, amphetamines and methylphenidate both reduced clinician-rated ADHD symptoms more than placebo in children, adolescents and adults, amphetamines by a slightly larger margin (SMD 0.24 to 0.29 more, low certainty, largely from indirect comparison); teacher ratings exist only for methylphenidate. Amphetamines led to more stopping because of side effects than placebo in both age groups and methylphenidate in adults only; the two did not differ significantly from each other in either age group. Both lowered weight and raised blood pressure slightly compared with placebo. There is no evidence beyond 12 weeks.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the efficacy differences favouring amphetamines head-to-head comparisons (PDF p. 1), but they are network estimates, and the authors themselves state that comparisons between drugs were frequently based on indirect evidence (PDF p. 9); in adults the network has no direct amphetamine–methylphenidate trials (Figure 2, PDF p. 4). The recommendation of methylphenidate as first choice in children and adolescents (abstract; PDF p. 9) rests on each drug's comparison with placebo for tolerability and acceptability (amphetamines worse than placebo, methylphenidate not), while the network estimate between the two drugs was not significant (OR 1.60, 0.94 to 2.73) and the Results state that no differences in tolerability were found between active drugs (PDF p. 7). The Interpretation correctly limits the conclusions to short-term treatment and calls for long-term research.

timeline.event: Protocol published (Cortese et al., BMJ Open; reference 30 of the review; not read)

Farhat et al., with authors in common, reused this review's original searches (to April 2017), updated them to January 2024 and analysed blood pressure, pulse and ECG measures by network meta-analysis

replication.where_it_stands: By its authors' account the most comprehensive synthesis of the short-term efficacy and tolerability of ADHD medicines up to its search date (PDF p. 8). Its search pool underlies Farhat et al. (2025), so the two are not independent evidence. For amphetamines against methylphenidate it gives a small, low-certainty efficacy advantage for amphetamines and no significant difference in stopping because of side effects.

Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: Double-blind head-to-head trials of an amphetamine against methylphenidate lasting a year or more, at doses optimized for each person, in children, adolescents and adults, reporting absolute rates of benefit, of stopping and of each side effect; and an individual-participant-data network meta-analysis of the existing trials, as the authors propose (PDF p. 2).

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Populations (children and adolescents; adults with ADHD), medicines, comparators (each other or placebo), outcomes and timepoints specified (PDF p. 3).

PROSPERO CRD42014008976 and a published protocol with planned subgroup and sensitivity analyses (PDF pp. 3–4). Changes to the protocol are listed on an appendix page that was not read, and a post hoc analysis is labelled as such, so whether every deviation is justified cannot be judged from the article.
Only double-blind randomized trials; enrichment designs excluded with a stated reason (PDF p. 3).

13 databases and registries including grey literature and dissertations, no language restriction, regulators' and manufacturers' websites, reference lists and contact with authors and manufacturers; search (April 2017) within 24 months of the analysis (completed February 2018) (PDF pp. 3–4).
Provisional: the article says data were extracted by at least two independent investigators but does not say how studies were selected; the protocol and appendix, not read, may say.
At least two independent investigators (PDF p. 3).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The article states that a list of excluded studies with reasons for exclusion is in the appendix (pp. 26–272) (PDF p. 4); the appendix was not read, so its completeness is unverified.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: the characteristics of the included trials are only in the appendix (pp. 283–381), not read; the article gives only counts of trials and participants by age group.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete data, selective reporting), with a strict overall rule (low only when every item is low): low in 23.5% of trials in children and adolescents and 27.5% in adults; unclear items fell from 63.5% to 35.2% after unpublished information was obtained (PDF pp. 5, 10).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Provisional: industry sponsorship was a planned effect modifier but could not be analysed (PDF p. 8); whether each trial's funding is listed can be judged only from the appendix, not read.

Random-effects pairwise meta-analyses and a frequentist network meta-analysis with a common heterogeneity parameter, allowing for multi-arm trials; inconsistency assessed locally (loop-specific approach) and globally (design-by-treatment model) (PDF p. 4).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis restricted to trials at low risk of bias was planned but could not be done for lack of data (PDF p. 8); no other analysis of the impact of risk of bias on the estimates is reported.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE ratings, which include risk of bias, are given for every comparison in Tables 1 and 2 and discussed, with low or very low certainty for most indirect comparisons (PDF pp. 6–8, 10).

Common heterogeneity SDs reported and compared with empirical distributions, subgroup and sensitivity analyses run where data allowed, and heterogeneity discussed (PDF pp. 7–9); the authors' argument that heterogeneity increases external validity is a judgment rather than an analysis.

The article states only that funnel plots are shown in the appendix (pp. 630–632); it reports neither their result nor a discussion of the likely impact of small-study or publication bias, and the limitations say only that missing information cannot be ruled out (PDF pp. 8–9).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funder's role and the authors' interests are declared (PDF pp. 4, 10).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One critical item is not met (15: no result or discussion of publication bias in the article), which by AMSTAR 2 gives low confidence; item 2 is partly met, items 4, 7, 9, 11 and 13 are met, item 12 is not met, and items 5, 8 and 10 can be judged only from the appendix. If the appendix reports and interprets the funnel plots, item 15 could become yes and the overall rating moderate. This rates the review's conduct as reported, not its value: the search, the systematic use of unpublished data and the GRADE ratings are strong. Cite for: short-term (about 12 weeks) estimates of efficacy and of stopping because of side effects for amphetamines and methylphenidate against placebo and against each other, with their certainty ratings. Do not cite for: long-term effects, absolute risks, rare harms, specific products or doses, or as head-to-head trial evidence in adults.

key_findings.finding: 133 double-blind randomized trials (81 in children and adolescents, 51 in adults, 1 in both) with 14,346 children and adolescents and 10,296 adults; the 12-week efficacy analysis included 10,068 children and adolescents and 8131 adults, the tolerability analysis 11,018 and 5362; unpublished data were used for 83% of trials.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Findings (PDF p. 1); Results, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Searches of 13 databases and registries from inception to 7 April 2017 without language restriction, plus regulators' and manufacturers' websites, reference lists and contact with authors and manufacturers; 9948 records screened, 3525 full texts assessed.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search strategy and selection criteria, 1st paragraph; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: Clinician-rated core symptoms against placebo: amphetamines SMD −1.02 (95% CI −1.19 to −0.85) in children and adolescents and −0.79 (−0.99 to −0.58) in adults; methylphenidate −0.78 (−0.93 to −0.62) and −0.49 (−0.64 to −0.35); all four of moderate certainty.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3A (PDF p. 5); Table 1, Placebo column (PDF p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamines against methylphenidate on clinician-rated symptoms: SMD −0.24 (−0.44 to −0.05) in children and adolescents and −0.29 (−0.54 to −0.05) in adults, both favouring amphetamines, both of low certainty.
Teacher ratings in children and adolescents: methylphenidate SMD −0.82 (−1.16 to −0.48, low certainty) against placebo; no teacher-rated data were available for amphetamines.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3B; Results, 4th paragraph (continuing on PDF p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Dropouts because of side effects against placebo: amphetamines OR 2.30 (1.36 to 3.89) in children and adolescents and 3.26 (1.54 to 6.92) in adults (moderate certainty); methylphenidate 1.44 (0.90 to 2.31, low) in children and adolescents and 2.39 (1.40 to 4.08, high) in adults.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3C (PDF p. 5); Table 2, Placebo column (PDF p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Amphetamines against methylphenidate on dropouts because of side effects: OR 1.60 (0.94 to 2.73, low certainty) in children and adolescents and 1.36 (0.54 to 3.43, very low) in adults, neither significant; the authors state that no differences in tolerability were found between active drugs in either age group.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, Amphetamines row, Methylphenidate column; Results, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Acceptability (leaving for any reason) was significantly better than placebo only for methylphenidate in children and adolescents (OR 0.69, 0.52 to 0.91) and for amphetamines in adults (0.68, 0.49 to 0.95). The CGI-I did not differ significantly between amphetamines and methylphenidate (no estimate given in the article).
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph (PDF p. 8); Discussion, 2nd paragraph, end (PDF p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Weight fell compared with placebo with amphetamines (SMD −0.71, −1.15 to −0.27, in children and adolescents; −0.60, −1.03 to −0.18, in adults) and with methylphenidate (−0.77, −1.09 to −0.45; −0.74, −1.20 to −0.28). Systolic blood pressure rose with amphetamines in children and adolescents (SMD 0.09, 0.01 to 0.18) and with methylphenidate in adults (0.17, 0.05 to 0.30); diastolic pressure with amphetamines (0.21, 0.12 to 0.31) and methylphenidate (0.24, 0.14 to 0.33) in the younger group and with methylphenidate in adults (0.20, 0.08 to 0.32). Blood pressure is given only as standardized differences, not in mm Hg.
key_findings.note: The text prints the age group of the first diastolic estimates as children and adults; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Post hoc, against placebo, dropouts because of side effects: lisdexamfetamine OR 2.69 (1.40 to 5.16) in children and 2.74 (0.80 to 9.30) in adults; other amphetamines 1.83 (0.84 to 4.02) and 3.66 (1.36 to 9.87). The authors draw no firm conclusion because few trials contributed.
key_findings.locator: Results, 12th paragraph (PDF p. 8); Discussion, 5th paragraph (PDF p. 9)

key_findings.finding: Too few trials reported outcomes near 26 or 52 weeks (all of them in adults) for analysis; the findings inform only short-term treatment.
key_findings.locator: Results, 14th paragraph (PDF p. 8); Discussion, 11th paragraph (PDF p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Most trials compared a drug with placebo and actual head-to-head trials were few, so comparisons between drugs were often indirect. In adults the network has no direct link between amphetamines and methylphenidate (both connect only to placebo); in children and adolescents some trials compared them directly.
Certainty (GRADE) of the primary-outcome comparisons: of 42 mixed comparisons, 13 very low, 18 low, 10 moderate and 1 high; of 59 indirect comparisons, 37 very low, 20 low and 2 moderate.

Risk of bias of the trials (overall low only when every item was low): children and adolescents 23.5% low, 65.4% unclear, 11.1% high; adults 27.5% low, 56.8% unclear, 15.7% high. Unclear items fell from 63.5% to 35.2% once unpublished information was gathered.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 5); Discussion, 10th paragraph (PDF p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity: common heterogeneity SD 0.355 (teacher ratings), 0.188 (clinician ratings) and 0.268 (tolerability) in children and adolescents, and 0.178 and 0.282 in adults; the test of global inconsistency showed no significant difference for the primary outcomes.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say diastolic blood pressure rose with amphetamines, atomoxetine and methylphenidate in children and adults, then give separate adult values for atomoxetine and methylphenidate only; the Discussion states that amphetamines raised diastolic pressure in children and adolescents but not in adults. The first age group appears to be a misprint for children and adolescents.
reporting_issues.consequence: The amphetamine diastolic estimate (SMD 0.21) should be read as applying to children and adolescents only.

reporting_issues.issue: The note to Figure 1 lists studies including patients with comorbid disorders among the main reasons for exclusion, while the Methods say comorbidities were not restricted except those needing concomitant medication.
reporting_issues.consequence: How far the results apply to people with ADHD and other conditions is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints guanfacine against placebo on teacher ratings (SMD −0.63, −1.62 to 0.35) in bold, the mark for significant results, although its interval includes zero; the text lists only methylphenidate and modafinil as superior to placebo on teacher ratings.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting error; not relevant to the comparison of amphetamines with methylphenidate.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls the efficacy differences favouring amphetamines head-to-head comparisons, but they are network estimates that rest largely on indirect evidence, and in adults on indirect evidence only.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should not describe these differences as results of trials comparing the two drugs directly.

verification.source_read: PDF of the online-first version (Lancet Psychiatry, published online 7 August 2018), PDF pp. 1–12 (all pages, including contributors, declarations, acknowledgments and references; text extracted and every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; the rotated Table 1 checked at 250 dpi and the network plots of Figure 2 at 300 dpi). Its page numbers 1–12 differ from the printed article (reference record, pp. 727–738), so anchors cite PDF pages. The appendix (cited in the article up to its p. 648) and the linked Comment were not among the files and were not read.
